strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important weakness in standard entropy-coded GPTQ: using a common quantization spacing across columns is suboptimal when activation covariance has uneven Cholesky diagonals. The resulting waterfilling-style rate allocation is simple, well motivated, and connects LLM PTQ to classical rate-distortion theory in a way that is genuinely useful.

The theoretical section provides a coherent asymptotic analysis under an iid Gaussian weight model, showing that PlainWaterSIC removes the AM-GM penalty incurred by Huffman-GPTQ and reaches a 0.255-bit high-rate gap to the waterfilling lower bound. The proof strategy and assumptions are mostly explicit.

Empirical results are promising: WaterSIC improves perplexity-rate frontiers on Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, and Llama-2-7B, with especially strong low-bit results. The appendix also includes downstream zero-shot evaluations and several diagnostics/ablations for the practical corrections.

The method is described in enough algorithmic detail to understand the main implementation, including calibration data construction, rate calibration, adaptive mixing, residual correction, diagonal rescaling, and entropy-rate accounting.
weaknesses: The central optimality claim is narrower than the title and abstract suggest. The 0.255-bit result is asymptotic, high-rate, and depends on iid Gaussian weights and large numbers of rows; it does not establish near-optimality for real LLM weights, low-bit regimes, nonlinear transformer behavior, or the heavily modified full WaterSIC pipeline used in experiments.

The empirical comparisons mix entropy-coded rates for WaterSIC/Huffman-GPTQ with log-cardinality rates for several baselines. This may be defensible, but it makes SOTA claims hard to interpret without actual compressed sizes, side-information accounting for all methods, and matched decompression/runtime constraints.

The final algorithm includes many practical heuristics beyond the theoretically analyzed core: LMMSE shrinkage, drift correction, residual stream compensation, diagonal row/column rescalers, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive golden-section tuning, dead-feature erasure, and Qwen-specific outlier row zeroing. The paper gives qualitative ablations, but not enough quantitative end-to-end PPL/accuracy ablations to isolate how much the waterfilling idea itself contributes.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Hyperparameters and procedures are described, but there is no clear code release statement, runtime cost report, random seed protocol, or full specification of baseline reimplementation versus copied results. The adaptive per-layer searches and model-specific row removal could be difficult to reproduce exactly.

The evaluation remains limited for a main-track SOTA compression claim: mostly WikiText-2 perplexity plus a small set of zero-shot tasks, no long-context or generation-quality evaluation, no 70B-scale experiment, and no end-to-end hardware benchmark for entropy decoding or inference throughput. The authors acknowledge some of these limitations, which is good, but they materially reduce the significance of the practical claim.

Presentation is generally clear but somewhat overclaims and contains several typos/notation issues. Some algorithm pseudocode appears to have indexing inconsistencies, and the impact statement is perfunctory despite the work enabling cheaper deployment of large models.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem in post-training weight quantization for LLMs: improving the rate-distortion tradeoff under activation-aware layerwise objectives. The motivation that equal bit allocation across input channels is suboptimal is clear and relevant.

The information-theoretic framing is a real strength. The paper connects GPTQ/ZSIC to lattice quantization and derives a clean high-rate comparison showing that the proposed per-channel spacing removes the AM-GM penalty suffered by entropy-coded GPTQ, leaving only the scalar quantization shaping gap of about 0.255 bits under the stated Gaussian/high-rate assumptions.

The proposed algorithm is conceptually simple at its core: use Cholesky/GPTQ-style successive cancellation but choose column spacings proportional to the inverse Cholesky diagonal. This is an intuitive and potentially useful modification to a widely used quantization pipeline.

The empirical results are promising. WaterSIC improves WikiText-2 perplexity over Huffman-GPTQ and several reported baselines on Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, and Llama-2-7B, especially in the low-bit regime, and the appendix includes useful zero-shot evaluations and ablations.

The paper is unusually explicit about several practical issues, including activation drift correction, residual-stream compensation, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure, entropy coding overheads, and layerwise rate calibration.
weaknesses: The central claims are stronger than the evidence supports. The title and text repeatedly suggest information-theoretic near-optimality, but the theorem applies to an iid Gaussian weight model, asymptotic high-rate/low-distortion limits, large row counts, entropy coding, and a layerwise Euclidean output objective. These assumptions are far from real LLM weights and from the downstream metrics used in the experiments.

The theory does not establish near-optimality for the actual full WaterSIC pipeline. Most practical gains appear to depend on additional heuristics: LMMSE shrinkage, diagonal row/column rescalers, Qronos-style drift correction, residual compensation, attention weighting, adaptive mixing, damping, and dead-feature erasure. The paper does not cleanly separate the theoretically motivated per-channel waterfilling idea from these substantial engineering additions in the main empirical claims.

The baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. WaterSIC and Huffman-GPTQ report entropy-coded rates, while several baselines report log-cardinality rates; some baseline results are taken from prior work rather than rerun under identical context length, calibration data, implementation, and evaluation settings. This weakens the claim of new state of the art.

The practical deployment story is incomplete. The method relies on entropy-coded variable-length integer weights and reports entropy or compressed storage, but it does not benchmark end-to-end decompression, inference latency, memory bandwidth, kernel support, or hardware integration. For LLM quantization, storage perplexity alone is not enough to demonstrate practical superiority.

The experimental evaluation is too narrow for the breadth of the claims. Most headline evidence is WikiText-2 perplexity at context length 2048, with downstream tasks relegated to the appendix. There are no large-scale models such as 70B, no code-generation/math/long-context evaluations, and limited analysis of cases where perplexity gains do or do not translate to task accuracy.

Several methodological choices raise reproducibility concerns. The paper gives many hyperparameters and algorithms, but the full implementation is complex and includes per-layer coordinate/golden-section searches, sampled-row binary searches, model-specific dead-feature handling, and Qwen-specific row zeroing. Without code and exact artifacts, reproducing the reported frontier would be difficult.

The Qwen3-8B treatment is concerning: manually identifying and zeroing specific outlier rows in the unquantized and quantized models before quantization is a model-specific intervention. Even if it has negligible perplexity impact, it complicates the interpretation of WaterSIC as a general post-training quantization algorithm.

The ablations are not sufficient to support the narrative. The appendix shows qualitative MSE plots for components, but the paper needs clearer quantitative ablations on final perplexity and downstream accuracy: plain WaterSIC versus full WaterSIC, with and without entropy coding, rescalers, drift correction, residual compensation, attention weighting, and adaptive mixing across multiple models and rates.

The limitations section is honest but too brief. It acknowledges lack of hardware benchmarking and larger-model experiments, but it does not sufficiently discuss the gap between the Gaussian high-rate theory and real LLM weights, possible overfitting to WikiText-2 calibration/evaluation, robustness to different calibration corpora, or the implications of variable-length compressed weights for serving.

There are presentation issues and some imprecision. The paper contains typos, inconsistent notation, and occasional overstatements such as broad SOTA claims despite mixed rate conventions and incomplete baseline control. The impact statement is generic and does not meaningfully discuss the environmental or misuse implications of making LLM deployment cheaper.

strengths: The paper offers a clear and useful conceptual contribution: it connects layerwise PTQ to rate-distortion theory and shows that unequal per-input-channel rate allocation, motivated by waterfilling, can close a gap left by entropy-coded GPTQ. The derivation that PlainWaterSIC has a 0.255-bit high-rate gap to the Gaussian information-theoretic limit is elegant and gives the algorithm a stronger foundation than many heuristic PTQ methods.

The empirical results are strong across several model families and bitrates. WaterSIC improves WikiText-2 perplexity over Huffman-GPTQ and other reported baselines on Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, and Llama-2-7B, with especially large gains at 1.5-2 bits. The zero-shot evaluations further support that the perplexity improvements are not purely metric-specific.

The manuscript is unusually transparent about practical engineering details. It specifies calibration data, damping, binary search, row sampling, adaptive mixing, residual-stream correction, dead-feature erasure, and side-information accounting, and includes algorithms and ablations/diagnostics for major components.

The work is significant for LLM compression: entropy-coded nonuniform quantization is a practical direction, and the paper provides both a principled explanation for why uniform GPTQ can be suboptimal and a method that appears to improve the compression-quality frontier without fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The central near-optimality claim is theoretically sound only under restrictive assumptions: iid Gaussian weights, high-rate/low-distortion asymptotics, sufficiently many rows for entropy coding, and a layerwise Euclidean objective. Real LLM weights and low-bit regimes are far from this setting, while the strongest practical results rely on several additional heuristics not covered by the theorem.

The comparison protocol is not completely uniform. WaterSIC and entropy-coded baselines report entropy-based rates, while some baselines report log-cardinality rates; some numbers are taken from prior work and may use different contexts or implementations. This does not invalidate the gains, but it weakens the force of broad SOTA claims.

The full method is complex, and the ablations mostly use relative MSE plots rather than end-task perplexity/accuracy for each component. It is therefore hard to disentangle how much of the final improvement comes from the waterfilling rate allocation versus activation drift correction, attention weighting, residual compensation, adaptive mixing, dead-feature removal, and model-specific outlier zeroing.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript alone. The paper provides many implementation details, but I did not see a code-release statement, exact baseline command/config parity, random seeds, compute cost, or wall-clock/runtime characterization. The method also appears computationally heavier than GPTQ due to repeated requantization and calibration forward passes.

The limitations section is honest but important: there is no end-to-end decompression/inference throughput evaluation, no hardware-kernel integration, and no experiments beyond 8B-scale models. Since entropy coding and side information are central to the method, real deployment performance remains an open question.
The impact statement is generic and does not discuss concrete risks or benefits of enabling cheaper deployment of LLMs. This is not a major ethical blocker, but the treatment is minimal.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and interesting idea: allocate quantization rate unevenly across input channels according to conditional innovation variances, connecting GPTQ-style sequential quantization to classical waterfilling and predictive rate-distortion theory.

The theoretical section is a meaningful contribution. Under the stated iid Gaussian/high-rate/asymptotic assumptions, the paper derives an information-theoretic lower bound, characterizes entropy-coded GPTQ, and shows that the proposed WaterSIC construction has only the scalar-lattice shaping gap of about 0.255 bits.

Empirical results are broad and promising: the method is evaluated on Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3-70B, with consistent perplexity improvements over Huffman-GPTQ and competitive or better results than several published PTQ baselines at 2-4 bits.

The appendices contain useful implementation detail, including calibration procedures, rate matching, damping, adaptive mixing, post-quantization finetuning settings, entropy-vs-codec checks, and several component diagnostics/ablations.
The paper is generally well motivated and connects an information-theoretic analysis to a practical LLM compression algorithm in a way that is more principled than many purely heuristic PTQ papers.
weaknesses: The central “information-theoretically near optimal” claim is much stronger than what is actually established for deployed LLMs. The proof applies to iid Gaussian weights, high-rate limits, asymptotically many rows, entropy-coded scalar/SIC quantization, and fixed covariance structure; the practical algorithm adds many heuristics whose effect is not covered by the theorem.

The empirical improvements are partly entangled with several additional techniques beyond the core WaterSIC rate allocation: activation drift correction, residual stream correction, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure, row/column rescalers, and optional finetuning. The ablations are helpful but mostly use relative MSE rather than final perplexity/accuracy, making it hard to quantify how much of the headline gain comes from the theoretically motivated idea.

Comparison fairness is imperfect. WaterSIC and Huffman-GPTQ report entropy-coded rates, while several baselines use log-cardinality or published numbers under potentially different implementations, calibration sets, context lengths, and finetuning protocols. This weakens the strength of the SOTA claims.

The practical method appears computationally complex, with per-layer secant searches, coordinate/golden-section searches for attention layers, repeated requantization, covariance collection from partially quantized models, and rescaler optimization. The paper does not provide a convincing cost comparison or end-to-end compression/decompression/inference throughput analysis.

Reproducibility is only moderate. Many hyperparameters are described, but the manuscript’s code link is a placeholder in the extracted text, and reproducing the exact results would require substantial implementation effort and access to specific calibration/evaluation pipelines.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The limitations section mentions hardware throughput and model scale but does not fully address the fragility of dataset-specific calibration/finetuning, the cost of extensive per-layer tuning, or possible downstream effects of compressing models used in sensitive deployments.

Some theoretical statements are slightly overgeneralized in presentation, e.g. claims for arbitrary PSD covariance matrices despite singular/near-singular cases requiring special handling, and high-rate formulae depending on positive eigenvalues/determinants. The paper handles dead features in practice but the theory/presentation could be more precise.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem, post-training weight quantization for LLM linear layers, and connects it to classical rate-distortion/waterfilling ideas in a way that is intellectually interesting.

The core intuition of allocating different effective rates to different input columns based on activation covariance structure is promising, and the paper gives a useful derivation relating GPTQ/SIC-style quantization to entropy-coded lattice quantization.
The empirical results are broad in model coverage for a PTQ paper, including Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, and appendix results on larger or older models, with comparisons across 1-4 bit regimes.

The paper includes several ablations and diagnostics in the appendix, discusses calibration context and calibration/finetuning data choices, and reports both perplexity and some zero-shot accuracy results rather than relying only on one metric.
weaknesses: There is a serious clarity and possibly correctness problem in the central rate-allocation description. The text claims the grid spacing should be proportional to the conditional activation standard deviation, while the distortion expression and Algorithms 2-3 imply the opposite dependence, alpha_i proportional to 1/L_ii. This is not a cosmetic issue: it is the main conceptual contribution and should be internally consistent.

The theoretical guarantee is much narrower than the paper's framing suggests. The 0.255-bit gap is derived under iid Gaussian weights, asymptotic high-rate/low-distortion assumptions, large row dimension for entropy coding, and positive-definite covariance behavior, yet the abstract and introduction present the result as broadly and uniformly applicable to linear-layer quantization.

The practical WaterSIC algorithm is substantially more complex than the clean theoretical method: LMMSE correction, activation drift correction, residual correction, row/column rescalers, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure, and optional finetuning. The paper does not isolate these components enough to show how much of the empirical gain comes from the claimed waterfilling idea versus accumulated engineering heuristics.

The experimental comparisons are not fully convincing. WaterSIC and Huffman-style baselines report entropy rates, while several competitors report log-cardinality bitwidths; this makes the Pareto comparisons hard to interpret as fair storage or deployment comparisons. The paper also does not demonstrate actual compressed file sizes, decompression cost, or kernel/runtime viability despite relying on entropy coding.

The SOTA claims are too strong for the evidence. Many baseline numbers are imported from prior work with potentially different calibration data, tuning protocols, context lengths, or implementation details, and the strongest WaterSIC-FT results include post-quantization finetuning of continuous parameters, which is not always matched by baselines.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code is available, but the experimental recipe still leaves important details unclear, including exact codec implementation, entropy estimation versus realized coding, hyperparameter searches for adaptive mixing, finetuning schedules across all models/rates, and whether all baselines were rerun under identical preprocessing and calibration.

The limitations section is too light. It acknowledges missing throughput evaluation and limited model scale, but does not adequately discuss fairness of entropy-rate comparisons, dependence on calibration/finetuning data, possible benchmark-specific tuning to WikiText-2 perplexity, or the gap between the Gaussian-weight theory and real trained LLM weights.

Presentation is uneven, with typographical errors, notation inconsistencies, and overbroad claims. These issues make it difficult to trust the central derivation without substantial repair, even though the overall idea is promising.

strengths: The paper offers a clear and meaningful conceptual contribution: it connects layerwise weight-only PTQ to rate-distortion theory and shows how unequal per-column rates motivated by waterfilling can improve over entropy-coded GPTQ. The theoretical result that PlainWaterSIC is within a 0.255-bit high-rate gap of the Gaussian information-theoretic limit is elegant and gives useful insight into why uniform-rate GPTQ can be suboptimal.

The empirical results are strong across several model families and scales. WaterSIC and WaterSIC-FT improve perplexity over Huffman-GPTQ, GPTQ/RTN variants, AWQ, QTIP, NestQuant, GPTVQ, and QuIP# in many matched-rate comparisons on Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-8B, Llama-3-8B, Llama-2-7B, and Llama-3-70B, with especially compelling gains at low bitrates.

The manuscript includes useful diagnostics and ablations for the practical additions beyond PlainWaterSIC, including LMMSE correction, activation drift correction, residual stream compensation, attention-weighted calibration, adaptive mixing, dead-feature erasure, and row/column rescalers. These make the method feel engineered rather than merely theoretical.

Reproducibility is better than average in terms of algorithmic detail: the paper gives pseudocode, calibration and finetuning protocols, hyperparameters, rate-targeting procedure, context lengths, datasets, and additional tables for C4, WikiText-2, KL divergence, and zero-shot tasks.

The limitations section is honest about important boundaries, including the focus on layerwise Euclidean post-matmul loss, the lack of end-to-end decompression/hardware throughput benchmarking, and uncertainty about scaling to larger models.
weaknesses: The strongest theoretical guarantee applies to an idealized high-rate setting with iid Gaussian weights and asymptotic entropy coding, while many of the headline empirical gains occur at 1-2 bits and rely on several additional heuristics. The paper could more sharply separate what is theoretically guaranteed from what is empirically effective in real LLMs.

The full practical algorithm is considerably more complex than the core WaterSIC idea. Several components require per-layer searches, adaptive mixing, drift/residual corrections, and model-specific handling; for example, Qwen3-8B uses manually identified outlier row zeroing. This raises concerns about robustness and ease of faithful reproduction across new architectures.

Some comparisons are not perfectly clean because WaterSIC reports entropy-based rates while several baselines use log-cardinality, and some baseline numbers are taken from prior work under potentially different implementation details. The authors acknowledge this, but it still weakens the evidential force of some SOTA claims.

WaterSIC-FT uses post-quantization finetuning of continuous rescalers and sometimes finetunes on datasets also used for evaluation-style perplexity reporting, so the FT variant should be interpreted separately from pure PTQ baselines. The paper mostly does this, but the headline comparisons sometimes mix PTQ and FT impressions.

The paper does not provide end-to-end inference measurements, decompression latency, memory-bandwidth effects, or kernel-level implementation evidence. Since entropy-coded weights are central to the claimed storage gains, practical deployment costs remain unresolved.

The impact statement is generic and does not meaningfully discuss possible downstream effects of enabling stronger model compression, such as broader deployment of capable models on constrained hardware. This is not a major blocker, but the ethics discussion is minimal.
